newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Boehringer eyes takeover, sees strong 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Boehringer eyes takeover, sees strong 1997.

text.p: Germany's privately owned pharmaceuticals giant Boehringer Ingelheim on Wednesday said it saw sales rising steeply in the next few years and signalled it was back on the aquisitions trail.
Officials declined to identify the current target of their attentions, but said a takeover could be sealed over the coming months.

"There are concrete discussions and they would have consequences in Germany as well as abroad," Heribert Johann, chairman of the group's management board, told a news conference after it posted sharply higher 1996 net profits.

The 112-year old group, which is among the world's 20 largest drug companies, has concentrated in the past on smaller alliances and takeovers, spending some 100 million marks ($58 million) on these last year. Company sources said that figure could rise signficantly in 1997.
Financing a large takeover will present few problems -- last year the group's reserves totalled 2.55 billion marks while cash flow rose nine percent to 834 million marks.
The group, reporting a 20 percent rise in 1996 net profits to 327 million marks, expressed confidence that it could convert promising research into higher revenues.
Johann said sales would climb by over 70 percent to 12 billion marks by the end of the century.
For the current business year, he said sales would rise six percent to 7.5 billion marks. First quarter sales had already outpaced year-ago levels by 13 percent.
"But of course we hope that we will be able to top our estimates, just as we did last year," Johann said.

Last year Boehringer posted a 10 percent rise in sales to 7.08 billion marks while net profit soared 20 percent to 327 million marks. "Overall we can be very satisfied with last year's results," Johann said.
The engine for growth was an 8.1 percent increase in volume sales and prices, the group said, saying acquisitions added 1.1 percent to the overall rise in sales.

Boehringer, whose single largest market is the U.S., also benefitted from the positive impact of a weaker mark in 1996, one year after a very weak U.S. dollar managed to severely dent most German drugs groups' results.

But a 15 percent rise in research and development costs to 1.2 billion marks and higher marketing costs related to new product launches forced last year's operating profit to fall by 3.5 percent to 651 million marks, Johann said.
Drug sales, rising over 10 percent to 5.96 billion marks, made up the lion's share of total turnover, trailed by chemicals, animal health and food additives.
The group's blockbuster respiratory drug, Atrovent, cleared sales of one billion marks last year.

Boehringer, like other German drugs companies, predicted that ongoing nervousness about Germany's health-care reforms -- which include a physician budget for prescription drugs -- would continue to weigh on domestic drug sales.
"In the first quarter, sales in Germany were about three percent below year ago levels," Johann said.

Looking ahead, board member Rolf Krebs said the group had several new products in the pipeline and that new launches should contribute significantly to the expected annual sales growth of 10 to 17 percent.
The group's rheumatism drug Mobic is expected to post sales of 750 million marks by the end of the decade.
-- Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.712 German Marks)
